new_statements.quote: Minor syllable are always stressless and never bear a distinct tone. Minor syllables are composed of an initial C and mid central vowel /ə/. The initial consonant of a minor syllable is generally a stop. Minor syllables are phonologically bound to a following major syllable. (Lar 2001, p27) [p. 99] ... Lar (2001) states that "all major syllables include a tone" (p27) [p. 98] ... Consonants which appear alone without any vowel signs or tone marks are unaccented syllables which are linguistically connected to the following syllable. They have a neutral vowel sound like the sound of the "a" in "about," and the tone is usually somewhere around mid tone. (Ballard 1993, p42) [p. 99] ... No coda is present, and the T is any of the six aforementioned tones. [p. 102]

new_statements.relation_note: The catalog record for Sgaw Karen has an empty rule. This work adds: tonal (six tones on every major syllable), no word-stress rule stated, minor presyllables stressless and toneless (quoted from Lar 2001). Nothing to contradict.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Sgaw Karen is a tone language: every major syllable carries one of six tones (in the consultant's dialect). The only stress-related statement is second-hand, quoted from Lar (2001) and Ballard (1993): minor (reduced /ə/) presyllables are 'always stressless' / 'unaccented' and toneless and are bound to the following major syllable, so prominence within a sesquisyllabic word lies on the tone-bearing major syllable. No word-stress placement rule is given for polysyllabic words; Fischer herself takes no position on the phonological status of minor syllables (she suggests the /ə/ may be epenthetic) and calls for further research.
new_statements.exceptions: None; the author says the criteria for minor syllables and their phonetic properties (duration, tone) remain to be established (p. 101).
new_statements.identity_note: Fischer 2013 describes the idiolect of one consultant, Ms. Tri Sa ('TS'), who grew up in Myeik (Mergui), Burma, lived 28 years in Mae Sot, Thailand, and then in Chapel Hill-Carrboro, North Carolina; the thesis compares her six-tone system with Moulmein and Bassein Sgaw (Jones 1961) and Yangon Sgaw (Lar 2001). Sarvestani 2018 describes the variety spoken in the Sgaw Karen refugee community of Buffalo, New York, and relates it to previously published varieties. Both are Sgaw Karen proper (sgaw1245), diaspora varieties.

new_statements.quote: Minor syllables lack codas and (in languages with weight distinctions) should be phonologically light. Minor syllables should lack stress and, in tonal languages, contrastive tones (Michaud, 2012). [p. 70] ... The status of these syllables is difficult to determine due to disagreement among linguists about what constitutes a minor syllable. Additionally, Sgaw phonology is not suited to making a well-motivated determination: the lack codas or obvious evidence of syllable weight or stress and the phonemic status of /ə/ complicate the matter. Finally, and importantly, if these syllables do constitute minor syllables in Sgaw, then they should lack tonal contrasts, putting them beyond the central focus of this dissertation. [pp. 70-71]

new_statements.rule_in_words: Sgaw Karen (Buffalo refugee-community variety) is a tone language with a 'Southeast Asian type of tone system' on a largely monosyllabic or sesquisyllabic lexicon; the dissertation states that Sgaw shows no obvious evidence of syllable weight or stress (and no codas), and remains agnostic on whether the reduced-/ə/ presyllables are true minor syllables. No word-stress placement is described.
new_statements.identity_note: Fischer 2013 describes the idiolect of one consultant, Ms. Tri Sa ('TS'), who grew up in Myeik (Mergui), Burma, lived 28 years in Mae Sot, Thailand, and then in Chapel Hill-Carrboro, North Carolina; the thesis compares her six-tone system with Moulmein and Bassein Sgaw (Jones 1961) and Yangon Sgaw (Lar 2001). Both are Sgaw Karen proper (sgaw1245), diaspora varieties.

tone_statements.quote: This instrumental study first describes the five lexical tones in S’gaw Karen and their interaction with breathy, creaky and modal phonation types. It is found that there is a phonotactic restriction on onset consonant and phonation. The combination of an aspirated onset with a breathy high tone is exceptionally rare and an aspirated onset does not co-occur with a breathy low tone.
tone_statements.summary: 5 lexical tones cross-classified by phonation (modal, breathy, creaky); onset aspiration x breathy-tone co-occurrence gap.

tone_statements.citation: West, Luke. 2016. Pitch specification of minor syllables in Sgaw Karen. Journal of the Acoustical Society of America 139(4, Supplement): 2218 (meeting abstract, 171st ASA meeting). doi:10.1121/1.4950643.
tone_statements.quote: Sgaw Karen is a Tibeto-Burman language with both lexical tone and a major-minor syllable divide. Unlike major syllables, minor syllables are structurally reduced and do not bear overt phonological tone. ... Analysis of minor syllable sequences adjacent to lexical tones shows (1) a low pitch target around 185 Hz to which minor syllables asymptotically approximate when given sufficient time, and (2) this target is not explicable by contextual interpolation.
tone_statements.summary: Lexical tone on major syllables; minor syllables toneless with a phonetic low pitch target.

tone_statements.citation: Jitwiriyanont, Sujinat. 2012. Ban Pa La-U Sgaw Karen Tones: An Analysis of Semitones, Quadratic Trendlines and Coefficients. MANUSYA: Journal of Humanities 15(2): 60-77.
tone_statements.quote: Each dialect of the Sgaw Karen language has a different tonal system. Despite the different number of tones, all of the previous studies agree on the fact that all tones of Sgaw Karen are level tones. However, according to my phonological analysis of the tonal system of Ban Pa La-u Sgaw Karen, this dialect has a contour tone. The tonal system comprises four tones, i.e. /low/, /mid/, /high/ and /falling/ occurring in nonchecked syllables. The high and low tones also have allotones in checked syllables.
tone_statements.summary: 4 tones: low, mid, high, falling (non-checked syllables); H and L allotones in checked syllables.
